#6095. Wow: Lufthansa Adds Premium Business Seats On Some Short Haul A320 Flights!

Lufthansa has just announced plans to introduce “real” business class seats on some of its narrow body planes, and that’s a really exciting development, given the typical business class standard on narrow body aircraft in Europe!

Interestingly, this is a concept that was initially trialed on Lufthansa Group low cost subsidiary Eurowings, and we knew at the time it was being used as a test for a more widespread implementation across the airline group. I’m delighted to see this become more widespread, and I hope this is just the start of a bigger trend.

Lufthansa has revealed that it will expand its premium offering on short and medium haul routes. With the introduction of the new Premium Business Seat, passengers will get more personal space than they’re used to on short haul aircraft.

Historically, business class on Airbus A320-family aircraft has consisted of standard economy seats with a blocked middle. So that means with the 3-3 layout, four seats were only sold per row. What’s happening is that the first three rows on some aircraft are being replaced with two rows of recliner seats, meaning the per-seat footprint is around 50% bigger than in standard business class.

At launch, the new Lufthansa Premium Business Seat will be available on six Airbus A320 aircraft (and these planes will also be equipped with Starlink). The seat will feature significantly more space, with nearly one meter of legroom, plus extra recline. This doesn’t replace the standard business class product, but instead, is an upsell option.

This new product is now available for sale for flights as of March 1, 2027, on routes between Frankfurt (FRA) and Athens (ATH), Cairo (CAI), and Nice (NCE). However, the first plane with the seats will already be in service as of December 16, 2026, and as of February 2027, it’ll be deployed on the above routes (but tickets are only on sale as of March as of now).

If a flight has this product available, you’ll see the “Premium Business Seat” designator during the booking process.

The process of actually booking a Premium Business Seat is essentially an upgrade cost on top of the standard business class fare. For example, looking at a Frankfurt to Athens route, I see an upgrade cost of €139, which frankly seems quite reasonable for a flight of this length.

Lufthansa is for the time being describing this as a commercial test, with the aim of examining demand for additional comfort on these routes, and the results will form the basis for deciding whether to expand the offering.

You’ll see many people refer to short haul business class in Europe as a “scam” (I don’t agree, but people say that), and they’re shocked to find economy seats with blocked middles. Admittedly product standards differ vastly around the globe.

The reason that airlines in Europe can get away with this product is threefold:

Keep in mind that most of the network carriers in Europe don’t make much money on short haul flights (or even lose a lot of money), given high costs and fierce competition from ultra low cost carriers.

With that in mind, I think Lufthansa is going about this exactly right:

I’d love to see more airlines introduce something similar. In particular, Air France, as Europe’s most premium airline, seems best positioned to do this, and could do it with very little opportunity cost. Why?

Honestly, if I were Air France, I’d just introduce this throughout the A220 fleet, and it would be a major point of differentiation, competitively. No airline could do it as efficiently as Air France, and every A220 flight has at least two rows of business class, so the opportunity cost is minimal.

Lufthansa will be introducing “real” business class seats on a subfleet of its Airbus A320s. As of the spring of 2027, expect these planes to be flying from Frankfurt to Athens, Cairo, and Nice. This Premium Business Seat concept will complement the existing business class, and will be available as a buy-up for business class passengers.

I’m very happy to finally see some more comfort on flights within Europe, and I imagine this will prove successful. If it doesn’t, I suspect it would be due to a lack of people knowing about this, rather than there not actually being demand.

What do you make of the Lufthansa Premium Business Seat concept?

#6094. Former United CEO Warns Airline’s AI Ban Could Drive Flyers Away—Its New Job Ad Shows What They Really Want

Former United Airlines CEO Oscar Munoz says customers who want an AI assistant to book their flights will choose an airline that lets them. That’s a warning to the airline he led, which just moved to ban those bookings. But the carrier’s own recruiting ad offers a revealing look at the future they’re preparing for: AI agents with access to shopping systems, under United’s control. Speaking with Scott McCartney on the November 15 special edition of Airlines Confidential, Munoz said: If travelers want an agent booking their trips, they’re going to find the airline that lets them do that.

Speaking with Scott McCartney on the November 15 special edition of Airlines Confidential, Munoz said:

If travelers want an agent booking their trips, they’re going to find the airline that lets them do that.

Munoz expects successful airlines to accommodate agents with safeguards and sees airlines negotiating terms of access, while recognizing that customers get a say in how they buy. That seems to focus on major labs, not offshore ones or open source.

United’s November 11 announcement cited account security, unintended purchases, misuse of miles and regulatory requirements. They said the restrictions would reach outside agents using United’s own systems as well as travel agencies and aggregators. As I wrote when United announced the ban, their contract language reaches even agents whose actions a customer supervises or approves. And current CEO Scott Kirby gave the real story, which wasn’t about security: To be honest, I don’t want to create another middleman.

United’s November 11 announcement cited account security, unintended purchases, misuse of miles and regulatory requirements. They said the restrictions would reach outside agents using United’s own systems as well as travel agencies and aggregators.

As I wrote when United announced the ban, their contract language reaches even agents whose actions a customer supervises or approves. And current CEO Scott Kirby gave the real story, which wasn’t about security:

To be honest, I don’t want to create another middleman.

An assistant that becomes the starting point for travel shopping can gain enormous bargaining power. It decides which options to recommend. Eventually, its owner might demand payment for access to customers. United would rather customers start with United where they can sell ancillaries as well as the ticket, control messaging to the customer, and manage costs.

United is banning agents at the same time they want to manage how they work with agents. A United Principal Developer – AI job listing describes connecting agents to flight shopping and shopping carts. Build reusable tools and APIs that expose existing business capabilities to authorized AI agents and applications.

United is banning agents at the same time they want to manage how they work with agents. A United Principal Developer – AI job listing describes connecting agents to flight shopping and shopping carts.

Build reusable tools and APIs that expose existing business capabilities to authorized AI agents and applications.

Human approval where appropriate, and recovery when something goes wrong. Controls over access, protection of customer information and safeguards for transactions. Testing and ongoing support for working systems.

A United assistant could be excellent at finding a United flight, explaining the seats and handling a schedule change. That would be valuable. But I wouldn’t expect it to suggest that I should buy a competing airline’s nonstop instead. An assistant working for me should know whether I’d pay more to avoid a connection, whether a better seat is worth the difference, and whether spending miles makes sense for this particular trip. It finds the best trip on the right airline to match my preferences and tradeoffs. I’ve made the same argument about rewards credit cards: companies are excited about using AI to sell more, but consumers get better tools, too. An offer that sounds appealing in an airline’s sales pitch may look much worse once software compares it with everything else available. Of course, the outside assistant might have its own conflicts. A service paid by airlines to produce bookings could favor whoever pays it the most. OpenAI’s Sam Altman says “If ChatGPT were accepting payment to put a worse hotel above a better hotel, that’s probably catastrophic for your relationship with ChatGPT.” He argued that a booking transaction fee would be acceptable if ChatGPT recommended the best choice independently and took the same cut regardless of what choice the customer books. My bet is that United eventually accepts more outside agents after negotiating terms, because customers will increasingly expect someone else to do this work. And they won’t be able to stop agents that book United tickets without paying them a separate fee or accepting their rules. There’s no world where passengers permanently abandon their preferred assistant to use an airline’s sales tool, and actually succeeding in blocking agents would cost United too much business. #6093. New Resy Rewards Program Offers 4x Bonus Amex Points For Dining Out

Resy has just launched the Resy Rewards program, which lets American Express card members in the United States earn an extra 4x points per dollar spent at participating Resy restaurants, on top of their credit card rewards. As you’d expect, it’s not quite that straightforward, but I’d still consider this to be pretty exciting!

American Express owns both Resy and Tock (which is now being integrated into Resy), as part of its larger “lifestyle” play for attracting card members. So along with that, Resy is leaning more into the rewards program side of things, with the new Resy Rewards program offering an extra 4x Amex points per dollar spent at eligible Resy restaurants.

Resy Rewards is first launching in New York City, where users will see a new “Rewards” tab within the Resy iOS app, where they can browse and book eligible restaurants. Restaurants participating in the Resy Rewards launch include Carne Mare, Le Crocodile, Hearth, Kiko, OPTO, Le Pavillon, and more. In 2027, Resy Rewards plans to expand to additional U.S. cities, and select Tock venues will become eligible to participate in the program.

So, how exactly does Resy Rewards work? Card members need to enroll a US-based Membership Rewards program eligible card in Resy Rewards, then book a Resy Rewards reservation through the “Rewards” tab in the Resy iOS app, and then pay the bill for the dining experience with the enrolled card. So this requires a little more jumping through hoops than just using an Amex card Resy credit, for example.

These rewards are in addition to whatever the standard rewards are on an Amex card. For example, the American Express® Gold Card (learn more) ordinarily earns 4x points at restaurants globally, so if you dined at a restaurant eligible for Resy Rewards, you could be earning 8x points per dollar spent, which is pretty awesome.

Here’s how Pablo Rivero, CEO of Resy and SVP of American Express Global Dining, describes this:

“For the first time, we’re bringing American Express’s industry-leading Rewards program into the Resy iOS app and connecting two things our Card Members value deeply: great dining experiences and meaningful rewards. As we’ve seen with the success of the Resy Credit, rewarding diners while driving demand and revenue to Resy restaurants is a win on both sides of the table.”

I’m delighted to see Amex introduce an opportunity to earn points for dining out, beyond the bonus categories already offered on some of the issuer’s most popular cards. For the time being, this is rather niche, given that it’s limited to select restaurants in New York City, but the expectation is that it will expand more broadly in 2027 (though it remains to be seen how broadly).

Essentially think of this as being similar to a dining rewards program, as the idea is that restaurants have to opt-in to participate in this, with the hope being that this drums up business for them (and presumably they pay Amex and Resy something extra in exchange for that).

Furthermore, you do have to specifically reserve your reservation through Resy to qualify for this, so if you don’t have a reservation made through the “Rewards” tab on Resy, then you won’t earn bonus points.

I’m happy to see this, as earning 8x points on dining when paying with the Amex Gold Card is quite a great deal. Then again, so much of my dining out is through InKind, which is my favorite dining rewards program, given the excellent selection of restaurants the program has in Miami, and it’s tough to compete with the rewards offered by the program.

The new Resy Rewards program offers bonus Amex points when you make a reservation at an eligible restaurant and then pay with your eligible Amex card. The idea is that you can earn an extra 4x points per dollar spent on purchases at eligible restaurants, which is pretty awesome.

The catch is that this is initially launching in New York City, only “eligible” restaurants qualify, and you need to reserve through Resy and then pay with the same linked card in order to earn the bonus points. It’s nice to see this launch, and I look forward to it expanding to more markets.

#6092. She Lived to the Sound of God’s Music

Remembering God’s gift to New York City girls and beyond.

From left: Sr. Christine Cosgrove, O.P., the author, Sr. Martha Kunesh, O.P., and speaker Kristen Hanson, an advocate against assisted suicide, at a National Review Institute/Sheen Center event on the virtue of hope.

Could anything sound more exotic today? This opening line comes from a 16th-century prayer by the Carmelite reformer St. Teresa of Avila. She carried it in the breviary she used for daily prayer. It also captures the quiet steadiness of Sister Martha Kunesh, O.P. (the initials stand for “Order of Preachers”), who entered a Dominican convent just before the opening of the Second Vatican Council. She took the religious name Sister Teresa Avila (“the ‘of’ was silent,” it was said). She eventually returned to her birth name, but she never lost the contemplative spirit of her first patron.

Starting a new LLC is exciting, but it also comes with lots of decisions, like how you'll manage your finances. A business credit card can help you separate your personal and company expenses while earning rewards on purchases you're already making. But getting approved can feel like a catch-22. You want a card to help establish your business credit history, but your LLC hasn't been around long enough to build one.

Fortunately, having a new LLC doesn't automatically rule you out of a Capital One business credit card. In fact, your personal credit history plays a significant role in determining which cards you qualify for, regardless of how long your company has been operating.

Whether you're just starting to build credit or have an established personal credit history, here's how to choose the right Capital One card for your LLC — and when it might make sense to move to one with better rewards.

Yes. You don't need years of business history to qualify for a Capital One business credit card.

When evaluating applications, Capital One considers several factors, including your personal credit history, income, business revenue and existing financial obligations. This is especially important for new LLCs that haven't yet established their own credit profiles.

For example, someone who formed an LLC last week but has excellent personal credit could qualify for a rewards card like the Capital One Spark Cash Select. Meanwhile, a business owner with a less-established personal credit history may have fewer options, even if their LLC is already generating revenue.

The key is understanding which cards you're most likely to qualify for and choosing one that fits your business's needs.

Related: How to apply for a Capital One business credit card

Capital One offers several business credit cards, ranging from simple cash-back options to premium travel rewards cards. Cash-back cards let you earn rewards you can use to offset business expenses, while travel rewards cards earn miles you can redeem for travel or transfer to airline and hotel partners.

Related: Getting started with points, miles and credit cards to travel

If you're starting an LLC and still building your personal credit history, the Capital One Spark Classic for Business is a good place to start. Unlike most Capital One business credit cards, which require excellent credit, the Spark Classic is designed for business owners with fair credit.

Who should apply? Spark Classic is a good fit for business owners who want to establish a positive credit history while keeping costs down. Although its rewards aren't as competitive as those of higher-tier cards, responsible use can help strengthen your credit profile and potentially open the door to more rewarding business cards down the road.

The card also reports account activity to personal credit bureaus, meaning your payment history and balances can affect your personal credit score. It offers useful business features, including free employee cards with customizable spending limits, virtual card numbers for vendor payments and year-end spending summaries to simplify bookkeeping.

The information for the Capital One Spark Classic card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been provided by the card issuer.

For new LLC owners who want to earn straightforward rewards without paying an annual fee, the Capital One Spark Cash Select is worth considering. The card also comes with tools to simplify everyday operations, including free employee cards with customizable spending limits and options for managing vendor payments.

Welcome offer: Earn $750 cash back after spending $6,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

Who should apply? The Spark Cash Select is a practical choice for new LLC owners with modest spending who prefer straightforward cash-back rewards. Although its 1.5% earning rate trails the 2% offered by Capital One's higher-tier cards, it's a solid option for businesses that want to earn rewards without paying an annual fee.

To learn more, check out our full review of the Capital One Spark Cash Select.

If you'd rather earn travel rewards than cash back, the Capital One VentureOne Business offers a way to accumulate miles without paying an annual fee. In addition to earning miles on everyday purchases, the card offers flexible redemption options, complimentary Hertz Five Star status* and no foreign transaction fees.

Welcome offer: Earn 50,000 bonus miles after spending $4,500 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

Who should apply? VentureOne Business is a good fit for new LLC owners who want to earn transferable miles without paying an annual fee. You can redeem miles toward travel purchases or transfer them to Capital One's 15-plus airline and hotel partners, potentially getting more value from your rewards.

The card also offers practical business features, including free employee cards with customizable spending limits, virtual cards for online purchases and Accounts Payable tools to help manage vendor payments.

The information for the Capital One VentureOne Business card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been provided by the card issuer.

*Upon enrollment, accessible through the Capital One website or mobile app, eligible cardholders will remain at that status level through the duration of the offer. Please note, enrolling through the normal Hertz Gold+ Rewards enrollment process (e.g., at Hertz.com) will not automatically detect a cardholder as being eligible for the program, and cardholders will not be automatically upgraded to the applicable status tier. Additional terms apply.

For LLC owners with growing business expenses, the Capital One Spark Cash offers a higher earning rate that could make paying an annual fee worthwhile. It also comes with helpful business features, including free employee cards, virtual cards for vendor payments and access to Capital One's Expense Management tool, which integrates with accounting software like QuickBooks and Xero.

Welcome offer: Earn a $1,000 cash bonus after spending $10,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

Annual fee: $0 introductory annual fee for the first year, then $95

Who should apply? The Spark Cash is a good fit for business owners whose spending is high enough to justify the annual fee. Compared with the Spark Cash Select, you'll earn an additional 0.5% cash back on everyday purchases. For example, an LLC spending $30,000 annually would earn $600 with the Spark Cash versus $450 with the Spark Cash Select, before accounting for annual fees.

To learn more, check out our full review of the Capital One Spark Cash.

For LLC owners who want to earn more travel rewards while enjoying additional perks and benefits, the Capital One Venture Business is an upgrade over the VentureOne Business. Along with flexible travel redemptions, the card offers complimentary Hertz Five Star status**, no foreign transaction fees and up to $120 in statement credits toward Global Entry or TSA PreCheck every four years.

Welcome offer: Earn 100,000 bonus miles after spending $10,000 on purchases within the first three months of account opening.

Who should apply? The Venture Business is a strong option for LLC owners who travel regularly and want to earn transferable miles on everyday business expenses. The card also offers a $50 annual Capital One Business Travel credit and up to $50 in annual statement credits for eligible advertising or software purchases, helping offset its annual fee.

Business owners can also take advantage of free employee cards and Capital One's Accounts Payable tools to help manage company spending.

To learn more, check out our full review of the Capital One Venture Business.

**Upon enrollment, accessible through the Capital One website or mobile app, eligible cardholders will remain at that status level through the duration of the offer. Please note, enrolling through the normal Hertz Gold+ Rewards enrollment process (e.g. at Hertz.com) will not automatically detect a cardholder as being eligible for the program and cardholders will not be automatically upgraded to the applicable status tier. Additional terms apply.

For LLC owners with substantial business expenses, the Capital One Spark Cash Plus offers greater purchasing flexibility while earning straightforward cash-back rewards. The card has no preset spending limit, meaning your purchasing power can adjust based on your spending behavior, payment history and credit profile. However, that doesn't mean unlimited spending.

Welcome offer: Earn a $2,000 cash bonus after spending $30,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening, plus an additional $2,000 for every $500,000 spent during the first year.

Annual fee: $150, refunded as a statement credit each year you spend at least $150,000 on purchases

Who should apply? The Spark Cash Plus is best suited to high-spending LLCs with strong cash flow. Although it earns the same 2% cash back as the Spark Cash, its larger welcome offer and potential annual fee refund make it particularly appealing to businesses that can meet the card's higher spending thresholds.

The card also includes free employee and virtual cards, Accounts Payable tools and access to Capital One's Expense Management platform, which integrates with accounting software like QuickBooks and Xero.

To learn more, check out our full review of the Capital One Spark Cash Plus.

Related: A guide to Capital One's Spark business cards

If you have excellent personal credit, there's no reason to settle for an entry-level business card just because your LLC is new. The Capital One Venture X Business is a premium option with valuable travel benefits, including airport lounge access, a $300 annual Capital One Business Travel credit and 10,000 anniversary bonus miles.

Welcome offer: For a limited time, earn up to 300,000 bonus miles and a $1,000 Capital One Business Travel credit:

Who should apply? The Venture X Business is best suited to LLC owners who travel frequently and have substantial business expenses. In addition to its top-tier travel benefits, the card offers no preset spending limit, free employee and virtual cards, and Accounts Payable tools to help manage company spending. Note that no preset spending limit is not equivalent to unlimited spending power.

However, businesses with more modest expenses may struggle to justify this card's $395 annual fee or meet the welcome offer's substantial spending requirements.

To learn more, check out our full review of the Capital One Venture X Business.

Yes. Capital One business credit cards generally require a personal guarantee, even if you're applying under your LLC's name.

A personal guarantee means you're personally responsible for repaying the card's balance if your business can't. This is particularly important for LLC owners, since forming an LLC generally provides some separation between personal and business liabilities.

In other words, applying with your LLC's employer identification number doesn't eliminate your personal responsibility for the account.

Yes. Capital One offers a business credit card preapproval tool that lets you see which cards you might qualify for without affecting your personal credit score.

The process uses a soft credit inquiry, so checking your options won't hurt your credit score. However, preapproval doesn't guarantee approval. If you proceed with a formal application, Capital One will perform a hard credit inquiry, which could temporarily affect your score.

Related: What credit card preapproval really means

You don't need years of business history to qualify for a Capital One business credit card. For LLC owners with fair credit, the Spark Classic offers a starting point for building credit while earning rewards. Those with excellent credit could qualify for higher-earning cards right away, even if their LLC is brand-new.

Ultimately, the best card depends on your credit profile, business spending and whether you prefer cash back or travel rewards.

#6090. Southwest’s New Credit Card Bonuses Offer Up To 90,000 Points Toward Companion Pass—Last Chance Before Rules Change

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

Southwest’s Companion Pass lets someone fly with you for just taxes and fees, even when you redeem points for your own ticket. For someone who flies Southwest with a partner a few times a year, it’s the single best deal in domestic air travel. And the easiest way to earn it is about to disappear.

There’s still a final window to use an 80,000- or 90,000-point credit card initial bonus toward a pass valid through December 31, 2027. You need to apply by December 2, 2026 and get approved. Neither bonus gets you all the way there on its own, but both give you a huge head start.

The Southwest Rapid Rewards® Priority Credit Card (See rates and fees) offers 90,000 bonus points after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening. It has a $229 annual fee. This is the premium Southwest co-brand card, really designed for folks who fly the airline. It makes those trips better, and spending helps earn both elite status and Companion Pass®. The travel benefits cover the cardmember and up to 8 additional passengers on the same reservation: First checked bag free. Preferred or Standard seat selection at booking, at no additional charge, when available. Extra Legroom seat upgrades within 48 hours of departure, at no additional charge, when available. Boarding with Group 5 or earlier if another benefit qualifies you for a better group. You earn 4 points per dollar on Southwest Airlines® purchases, including flights, inflight purchases and Southwest gift cards; 2 points per dollar at gas stations and restaurants; and 1 point per dollar on other purchases. There are also 7,500 anniversary points each year. The Southwest Rapid Rewards® Plus Credit Card (See rates and fees) offers 80,000 bonus points after spending $1,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening. Its annual fee is $99. That’s a much lower spending requirement for a bonus that’s only 10,000 points smaller. First checked bag free for the cardmember and up to 8 additional passengers on the same reservation. Standard seat selection within 48 hours of departure, when available, for the same group of travelers. Group 5 boarding or earlier if you otherwise qualify. 3,000 anniversary points each year, plus a 10% anniversary flight discount code that excludes Basic fares. The Plus card earns 2 points per dollar on Southwest Airlines® purchases, and 2 points per dollar at gas stations and grocery stores on the first $5,000 in combined purchases per anniversary year. Other purchases earn 1 point per dollar. I’d choose Plus for the lower cost of getting the bonus. Priority costs $130 more per year, but gives you better seat benefits, 4,500 more anniversary points and a larger initial bonus. For a family that flies Southwest regularly, those seating benefits can easily be worth the difference. How Close These Bonuses Get You To Companion Pass Under the 2026 rules, earning 135,000 Companion Pass qualifying points in a calendar year gets you the pass for the rest of that year and the following year. Southwest credit card customers receive a 10,000-point qualifying boost, so they effectively need 125,000 more. Priority: 90,000 bonus points plus the 10,000-point boost gets you to 100,000. You need another 35,000 qualifying points. Plus: 80,000 bonus points plus the 10,000-point boost gets you to 90,000. You need another 45,000 qualifying points. The purchases you make to earn the bonus also earn points. Assuming those purchase points post in 2026, spending the minimum at 1 point per dollar reduces the remaining gap to 32,000 points with Priority or 44,000 with Plus. Bonus category spending and qualifying points you’ve already earned reduce it further. Qualifying flights and eligible partner activity can help fill the gap, too. Check your Companion Pass progress in your account. Once you have the pass, book your own Southwest flight with cash or points and add your designated companion, as long as there’s an available seat. Their taxes and fees start at $5.60 one-way. You can use the benefit repeatedly and change your designated companion up to three times per calendar year. How Optimal Timing Of The Companion Pass Has Changed As I covered in Southwest’s 2027 Rapid Rewards overhaul, unlimited Companion Pass becomes a benefit of the new Platinum elite tier next year. Initial bonuses generally stop helping you qualify. Anniversary points, referral bonuses and extra points from card bonus categories stop counting, too. Southwest’s transition exception preserves the initial bonus for customers who apply by December 2, 2026, are approved, and meet the offer’s requirements. Even if you finish the required spending in early 2027, the bonus can count toward 2026 qualification for a pass ending December 31, 2027. So the old strategy of waiting until January to earn nearly two years of Companion Pass doesn’t work here. A bonus earned under this exception won’t get you a pass through the end of 2028. And Chase’s terms distinguish the initial bonus from ordinary purchase points. Those purchase points must post to your Rapid Rewards account in 2026 to count toward this pass. Spending after your December statement closes generally posts in January. You also want the 10,000-point qualifying boost credited in 2026; Southwest allows up to 30 days after account opening for it to arrive. You still have to meet the initial bonus spending requirement within the first 3 months from account opening. The transition rule doesn’t extend that deadline. I’m a former Companion Pass holder, and a promotional Companion Pass holder.Southwest still represents about 40% of the seats out of my home airport in Austin. Even with all the changes they’ve made, being able to bring someone along on those flights for just the taxes is huge. Before applying, you can’t currently hold a Southwest personal credit card, and you can’t have received an initial bonus on any Southwest personal card in the past 24 months. Southwest business and employee cards are excluded from that restriction. Chase’s usual 5/24 rule also applies: generally, you need fewer than 5 new credit card accounts on your credit report in the past 24 months. If you’re eligible, can handle the required spending, and have a path to the remaining qualifying points, I’d take advantage of this before December 2. #6089. Singapore Airlines Cuts Elite Upgrade Rewards For 2027—And Halves The Time To Use Several Smaller Perks

Singapore Airlines is cutting the upgrade certificates its biggest spenders earn from three to one for every 100,000 PPS Value, starting January 1, 2027. Regular KrisFlyer members lose both of their milestone upgrades. And several smaller rewards will expire in six months instead of a year. They’re replacing most of the upgrades with mileage discounts. Those will be more useful to members who couldn’t use their certificates, and there’s an improvement for unused PPS upgrades. But the package reduces the upside of being especially loyal to Singapore Airlines. The airline’s announcement also includes a doubled service fee, ScootPlus awards, and a replacement for the KrisShopper shopping program. KrisFlyer Loses Both Milestone Upgrades KrisFlyer Milestone Rewards are earned by regular, Silver and Gold members based on eligible Elite miles accumulated during the calendar year. Singapore Airlines and Scoot flights count. Partner airline flights don’t, even when they count towards elite status. Eligible spending through Kris+, KrisShop and Pelago can contribute, but only up to 5,000 Elite miles for regular and Silver members, or 10,000 for Gold. Elite Miles   2026 Reward   2027 Reward 1,000   1,000 bonus miles on next Scoot flight + 40% Pelago discount   40% Pelago discount 2,500   20% Scoot discount   1,000 bonus miles on next Scoot flight 5,000   1,000 KrisPay miles   S$20 KrisShop discount 7,500   —   20% Scoot discount 10,000   S$20 KrisShop discount   2,000 KrisPay miles 15,000   —   1,000 bonus miles after qualifying ground purchase 20,000   25% bonus miles on one flight segment   Unchanged 30,000   50% bonus miles on one flight segment   Unchanged 40,000   5,000-mile redemption discount   Unchanged 60,000   Double miles on one flight segment   Unchanged 75,000   Short haul advance upgrade   10,000-mile redemption discount 100,000   Economy to premium economy advance upgrade   20,000-mile redemption discount Rewards through the 15,000 Elite mile level will have six month validity. The existing Scoot rewards and KrisShop coupon currently last a year. Pelago improves from three months to six. Rewards at 20,000 Elite miles and above keep their twelve month validity. The 40% Pelago discount is capped at S$20. The S$20 KrisShop coupon requires a S$50 purchase. The Scoot discount applies to the base fare, rather than the entire ticket price. The 2,000 KrisPay miles are app spending credit, not 2,000 airline miles you can move into KrisFlyer. You have six months to claim them, then six months to spend them. The new 1,000-mile bonus requires at least S$10 in a qualifying transaction. For a Pelago experience, the activity must also be completed within the reward’s validity. The Scoot discount now takes three times as many Elite miles to earn, and you get half as long to use it. Moving it to 7,500 also puts it beyond the 5,000 miles that regular and Silver members can count from ground spending alone. The old certificates required an eligible paid fare and available upgrade space. The 75,000-mile reward was restricted to specified short routes, and the 100,000-mile reward only moved you from coach to premium economy. Solitaire PPS Members Give Up Two Of Three Upgrades PPS Club is Singapore’s separate program for premium cabin customers. PPS Value generally tracks Singapore dollar spending on business class, first class and Suites, excluding airport taxes. Limited ground spending also counts. The 30,000 and 40,000 PPS Value rewards stay the same. The changes above those levels affect Solitaire PPS Club members. The schedule repeats with each 100,000 PPS Value, up to 500,000 per membership year. That cuts the maximum number of upgrade certificates from fifteen to five. An established Solitaire member earning 60,000 to 69,999 PPS Value in a membership year loses the upgrade at 60,000 and gets no replacement. Someone who reaches 100,000 gets three separate 50,000-mile discounts plus one upgrade, or five discounts if they convert that upgrade. Those successful at turning eligible paid business class fares into first class or Suites lose valuable opportunities. Unused PPS Upgrades Get A Second Life From January 1, a still-valid, unused PPS advance upgrade can be converted into two separate 50,000-mile redemption discounts. If you leave it unused, conversion happens automatically at expiry. The replacement discounts get a fresh twelve months. That includes eligible certificates earned in 2026 at 60,000, 75,000 and 100,000 PPS Value. Higher Fees, ScootPlus Awards And A Shopping Program Replacement Starting December 1, 2026, the offline service charge doubles from US$25 or 2,500 miles to US$50 or 5,000 miles. This is an additional service charge, separate from applicable change or redeposit fees. ScootPlus awards are coming in early 2027, bookable through Scoot’s website or app. Prices haven’t been announced. Meanwhile, KrisShopper will close in January, with members automatically enrolled in a new program covering KrisShop, Kris+ and Pelago. Existing vouchers remain valid until their expiration dates, and KrisFlyer miles and status credits already earned remain in members’ accounts. #6088. Standing Athwart Pumpkin Tyranny

Through October and November, this mediocre flavor and scent are in everything everywhere all the time.

A display of Trader Joe’s pumpkin and fall-themed products at a grocery store in Lafayette, Calif., September 25, 2026.

A pumpkin spice latte is on the menu at every coffee shop. Sometimes, the drink is served in a pumpkin-shaped mug. To lure in customers for brunch, quaint cafes serving pumpkin pancakes put a chalkboard sign on the sidewalk saying, “COME IN FOR GOURD VIBRATIONS!” Each bakery has pumpkin scones, pumpkin pie, pumpkin banana bread, and pumpkin coffee cake. An attempt to order an old fashioned will be met with an invitation from the demoralized bartender, “Do you want to try our pumpkin spice old fashioned?” The pen at the bank is topped with a rubber pumpkin; this way, customers know that all the money is kept safe. Little plastic pumpkins are in the windows displays at clothing shops, or beside the cashiers (who work in front of pumpkin-flavored nicotine patches). Squashes are piled high in cardboard bins by the entrance of every grocery store. I reach for what I think is my favorite chai tea blend on the shelves — but alas! It is now pumpkin chai with an orange label.

Through October and November, pumpkin is in everything everywhere all the time. Anything edible is infused, swirled, drizzled, and dusted with pumpkin. You cannot escape the flavor: pumpkin cereal, pumpkin protein powder, pumpkin bagels with pumpkin cream cheese. The Asian aisle has frozen Kung Pao-mpkin Dumplings. Dog treats are flavored like a pumpkin spice latte because everyone must participate, no exceptions. Longstanding favorites are replaced, so French fries are now pumpkin fries. That peculiar squash always sneaks its way into a dish, and so the stuffed raviolis have a little bit of pumpkin. Despite its omnipresence, the pumpkin surprises you: The waiter arrives at the table with a salad that is topped — just for this week — with toasted pumpkin seeds. (Of course, the utensils are wrapped in a flimsy brown napkin dotted with little orange pumpkins.) Even things we thought were reliably mint, like gum and the dentist’s fluoride, are pumpkin spice.

Abigail Anthony is a staff writer at National Review.

#6087. American Airlines Replaces Its Rebooking Cards—Agents Now Must Do More Than Hand Them To Stranded Passengers

American Airlines is replacing the cards it hands passengers when their flights fall apart. The new Travel Assistance Card points customers to rebooking, baggage tracking, eligible vouchers and other help. And employees are being told to do more than hand over the card and send passengers away. An internal memo set this week as the start date at domestic airports. Use the Travel Assistance Card as a guided customer support tool, not simply as a handout. That’s a small change in what American hands customers, with a much bigger expectation for what employees are supposed to do. What Replaces The RICAP Card I’ve written about American’s RICAP cards and the special phone number printed on them. The name stands for Reservations Irregular Ops Customer Assistance Program. Airport agents gave them to customers affected by delays and cancellations, providing a way to get rebooked when airport lines were long. American periodically changed the number. They didn’t want it becoming everyone’s everyday reservations shortcut, and employees had to throw away old cards so they weren’t sending stranded passengers to a disconnected line. The old cards already had QR codes. The change here is a broader set of resources and instructions for how employees should use the card. The new version provides web addresses and QR codes for: Rebooking and baggage tracking. Eligible vouchers and refund information. Answers to common questions, chat support, the American Airlines app and additional travel assistance. Employees are told to offer it during cancellations, significant delays, missed connections, weather events and other operational disruptions. They’re supposed to explain how to scan the code or use the web address, then help the passenger identify which resources address their problem. Domestic mainline and regional stations are instructed to switch once their new cards arrive and discontinue all previous RICAP cards. International stations keep using RICAP. American Has Been Building More Ways To Recover From A Disruption This fits a series of changes at American: January’s disruption screens brought clearer status banners alongside rebooking, bag tracking and digital vouchers in the app and on the website. Agents gained the ability to issue meal vouchers to an entire eligible flight, rather than processing everyone individually. In June, automatic meal vouchers expanded beyond elite members to all AAdvantage members. Earlier this month, American added standby inside its disruption rebooking tool. Passsengers can try for an earlier nonstop while keeping their confirmed replacement flight until standby clears. The latest hotel and transportation update described automatic offers for qualifying overnight delays and an Uber Central rollout allowing authorized agents to arrange rides without passengers downloading Uber. American’s January app screens show the resources this card is meant to help passengers find: This Is Part Of Becoming An Airline People Will Pay More To Fly American has been adding better seats, lounges and food. Their premium push also depends on what happens to passengers whose flights don’t run on time. Robert Isom included disruption recovery technology in his plan to reclaim American’s premium reputation. And Chief Customer Officer Heather Garboden has put the value of a one point improvement in net promoter score at $50 million to $100 million in revenue. A passenger who gets rebooked quickly and into a hotel can still be willing to buy American again. Spending hours in a line, then discovering that nobody can help, undermines the rest of the money they’re spending on the product. They’ve also been trying to reduce the disruptions themselves. American spread Dallas–Fort Worth’s schedule across 13 smaller connecting banks instead of nine. Management reported missed connections down 50% in the early April results. American’s overall reliability still doesn’t outperform though. In the September performance figures I covered, American arrived on time 77.11% of the time, compared with 78.65% for United and 82.52% for Delta. And American has been working against itself in how it handles passengers. I covered the loss of routinely staffed customer service counters at Washington National, where passengers were directed to digital tools and phones, with live help brought out during major disruptions. The new instruction to guide passengers through the card makes sense. Someone who can’t get the app to offer a workable itinerary still needs an employee’s help. At a gate with one employee, though, boarding the next departure and walking several stranded customers through their options compete for the same person’s time. This memo gives that employee another task. It doesn’t add anyone else to help. The new instruction to guide passengers through the card makes sense. Someone who can’t get the app to offer a workable itinerary still needs an employee’s help. At a gate with one employee, though, boarding the next departure and walking several stranded customers through their options compete for the same person’s time. This memo gives that employee another task. It doesn’t add anyone else to help. I’ve written about American’s RICAP cards and the special phone number printed on them. The name stands for Reservations Irregular Ops Customer Assistance Program. Airport agents gave them to customers affected by delays and cancellations, providing a way to get rebooked when airport lines were long.

American periodically changed the number. They didn’t want it becoming everyone’s everyday reservations shortcut, and employees had to throw away old cards so they weren’t sending stranded passengers to a disconnected line. The old cards already had QR codes. The change here is a broader set of resources and instructions for how employees should use the card.

The new version provides web addresses and QR codes for:

Employees are told to offer it during cancellations, significant delays, missed connections, weather events and other operational disruptions. They’re supposed to explain how to scan the code or use the web address, then help the passenger identify which resources address their problem.

Domestic mainline and regional stations are instructed to switch once their new cards arrive and discontinue all previous RICAP cards. International stations keep using RICAP.

This fits a series of changes at American: January’s disruption screens brought clearer status banners alongside rebooking, bag tracking and digital vouchers in the app and on the website. Agents gained the ability to issue meal vouchers to an entire eligible flight, rather than processing everyone individually. In June, automatic meal vouchers expanded beyond elite members to all AAdvantage members. Earlier this month, American added standby inside its disruption rebooking tool. Passsengers can try for an earlier nonstop while keeping their confirmed replacement flight until standby clears. The latest hotel and transportation update described automatic offers for qualifying overnight delays and an Uber Central rollout allowing authorized agents to arrange rides without passengers downloading Uber. American’s January app screens show the resources this card is meant to help passengers find: This Is Part Of Becoming An Airline People Will Pay More To Fly American has been adding better seats, lounges and food. Their premium push also depends on what happens to passengers whose flights don’t run on time. Robert Isom included disruption recovery technology in his plan to reclaim American’s premium reputation. And Chief Customer Officer Heather Garboden has put the value of a one point improvement in net promoter score at $50 million to $100 million in revenue. A passenger who gets rebooked quickly and into a hotel can still be willing to buy American again. Spending hours in a line, then discovering that nobody can help, undermines the rest of the money they’re spending on the product. They’ve also been trying to reduce the disruptions themselves. American spread Dallas–Fort Worth’s schedule across 13 smaller connecting banks instead of nine. Management reported missed connections down 50% in the early April results. American’s overall reliability still doesn’t outperform though. In the September performance figures I covered, American arrived on time 77.11% of the time, compared with 78.65% for United and 82.52% for Delta. #6086. “The sitting president doesn’t win”: Ahead of midterms, Trump reflects on himself

On the last day before the 2026 midterm elections, President Donald Trump gave a speech before the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, a site of considerable scandal in his second term. He joked it should be renamed after him and spent considerable time discussing Washington, D.C. construction projects and resurrecting conspiracy theories about monument vandals. When the president did turn to the elections, more than 23 minutes into an hour-long speech, he seemed to foreshadow major Republican losses in the House and Senate, describing it as “The most important midterm, I believe, in our lifetime.”

“When you vote, remember a party that hates America cannot be allowed to rule over the people who built our country,” Trump said, referring to Democrats, whom he said want to “blow all of this up by electing communist jihadists.”

“If the people that voted for me and voted in the last election where we had such a great victory, if they go out and vote, just a good portion of them, we will win in a landslide,” Trump said midway in his speech. “Now that doesn’t happen because usually whoever the sitting president is, Republican or Democrat, uh, good or bad, good president, great president, bad, for some reason the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms, but we gave this a very strong shot.”

The last day of polling indicates that Democrats have odds that are better than good to flip control of the House and Senate. The final results from the New York Times/Siena University polls report “The party is ahead in all seven states likeliest to decide control of the Senate: Michigan, Kansas, Texas, Maine, Ohio and, more narrowly, Alaska and Iowa.” The final predictions in the Cook Political Report included five additional shifts for Democrats in North Carolina, Florida, Tennessee and Virginia, projecting “that Democrats will win 15 to 25 seats, putting them at a 230- to 240-seat majority.” If a sweep happens in the toss up races, it’ll give Democrats their strongest majority since 2009.

Meanwhile, early voting records have been smashed around the country, in places like South Carolina and Ohio. In Texas, more than 7.7 million voters did so early, surpassing the record turnout for a midterm election set in 2018. Across the nation, about 50 million ballots have already been cast so far, with the share of registered Democrats notably increased in several key state races. But according to the New York Times, around half the expected votes will come on Election Day itself, making it difficult at this point to determine how big a role early votes will play in the outcome.

#6085. Airbnb Updates House Rules After Host Pushback

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: An Airbnb superhost and guest in Chicago. Airbnb

Hosts got through to Airbnb on their complaints and Airbnb made changes. But most of the policies that stoked host anger, such as a limit on guest checkout chores, a ban on contracts, and collecting guest IDs, remain in place.

Airbnb updated the House Rules policy it announced in October that limits what hosts can ask of guests. Under the November 3 changes, hosts can now detail Additional rules at checkout that were previously called Requests.

There is no change in the substance, however. Guests can be encourage to put dishes in the sink and collect used towels, but they can't be required to wash the dishes and do the laundry.

"Some of you are concerned about losing control over the rules you set for your home,” the company wrote in the update. “We understand why. You’re opening your home to guests, and you should be able to expect them to treat it with respect. We also could have done a better job explaining why and how we’re making these changes.”

A general restriction on contracts between hosts and guests, and a prohibition against collecting guest IDs — both of wh

Airbnb has partially walked back a House Rules policy announced in October after hosts objected publicly, but the core restrictions take effect as planned on November 20. Under the November 3 update, what Airbnb had called "Requests" — instructions guests were only "encouraged" to follow — are now "additional rules" that guests "are expected to comply with," covering items such as putting dishes in the sink, gathering used towels, and sorting recycling. Hosts can also require a separate rental agreement when an insurer demands one, alongside existing exceptions for laws, homeowners associations, and building rules. Airbnb published a review timeline for the first time: listing reviews begin November 20 and run through March 2027, with at least 20 days to fix a flagged rule and one appeal per rule, supporting documents allowed. The limits that drew the most attention remain: no checkout chores such as washing dishes or stripping beds, no host-imposed fines, no rules added after booking, and no collecting guest IDs, emails, phone numbers, or signed agreements absent a legal, building, or insurer requirement. Hosts can cancel without penalty only when a guest breaks one of the seven standard rules. Airbnb declined to comment for this story.

For years, the travel industry has been embracing artificial intelligence, using it to make websites easier to digest — and even generate personalized recommendations. Now, it has become an invaluable tool for travelers searching for the best Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals.

Experts told TPG that using AI can make the start of trip planning feel less daunting and more natural. In fact, travelers can ask for a list of hotels within a certain budget range, and that happen to be close to things like public transport or have perks like free breakfast, said Melanie Fish, a travel expert at Expedia.

“Instead of starting with a long list of filters, travelers can tell [sites like] Expedia or Hotels.com what they have in mind, in their own words,” Fish said. “AI can help them explore hotel options, compare what matters and narrow the choices.”

At Hotels.com, the company offers a “Natural Language Search” for Black Friday travel deals, allowing travelers to search for things like “‘Four nights in Barcelona in May on sale for Black Friday or Travel Tuesday,’ and get hotels offering up to 50 [percent] off,” Fish said.

Ian Ackland, the managing director for the Americas at Booking.com, recommended travelers start their prompt with the kind of trip they want, rather than just searching by the discounts that pop up post-Thanksgiving. That’s because what constitutes a “good deal” may mean more than simply a cheap rate.

“Share your destination, dates, budget and the details that matter, like breakfast, family space or walkable restaurants,” Ackland said. “The more specific you are, the more useful the results can be. A good deal is one that fits the trip, not one that’s simply the lowest price.”

Related: How AI is transforming the future of travel

It can also be used for side-by-side comparisons of different hotel options, said Google spokesperson Sarah Armstrong. At Google, the AI assistant Gemini can pull everything from base rates to estimated taxes, resort fees, cancellation policies and more.

The AI tool can also save time by continuing to work in the background with things like price alerts while travelers focus on other things.

“When you're ready to secure your room, Auto Browse in Gemini in Chrome can take the wheel,” Armstrong said. “Working right from the Chrome side panel, Gemini can navigate travel sites, fill in your dates and select your room options then pause safely at the checkout screen so you can review the final details before paying.”

That said, AI isn’t full proof. That’s especially true with Black Friday deals since prices can change quickly and promotional terms vary, Fish said.

“Tools like Claude and ChatGPT can be a useful shortcut, but travelers should treat its recommendations as a starting point, not the final source of truth,” Fish said. “Potential pitfalls include outdated or incomplete pricing, missed taxes and fees, limited availability, incorrect details about amenities or cancellation policies, and recommendations that don’t reflect the traveler’s priorities.”

Ackland said Booking.com has worked with AI for over a decade, and ultimately, it “should help you make a decision, not leave you guessing about what you’ve booked.”

It is important to note while AI tools do “occasionally get things wrong,” Armstrong said, it won’t make purchases without permission. Nonetheless, “it's still smart to review the key details like dates, prices, and cancellation rules before hitting confirm.”

Thankfully, Fish said picking whether travelers use AI or a traditional search engine doesn't have to be “an either-or choice.”

“AI is particularly useful for inspiration and discovery,” Fish said, “while traditional search and trusted travel platforms… remain the best places to confirm live prices, availability, sale terms, guest reviews and cancellation policies — and to complete the booking.”

#6083. Delta CEO’s Cope: Ed Bastian Says Doesn’t Need Starlink, Current Wi-Fi Good Enough

Delta Air Lines CEO Ed Bastian says “customers are not choosing airlines based on the Wi-Fi.” That’s a remarkable claim from an airline that’s spent years promoting free internet as a reason to choose its premium experience. Speaking at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit on Monday, Bastian defended passing on Starlink and waiting for Amazon Leo which is still unproven and whose timetable is now in question. He downplayed competitors’ progress, argued Delta’s current Viasat service comes close enough, and expressed confidence that Amazon would match or beat Starlink. It was pure cope. Delta doesn’t plan to begin installing Amazon until 2028 and that’s if the service works and delivers on schedule. United and Southwest both plan to finish their Starlink installations in 2027, and American is adding the service as well (so are Alaska and even Frontier). Delta’s Wifi Was Fine When Fewer People Used It Delta’s Viasat internet was fine when a few people on each flight were paying to use it. Make it free, get a much larger share of the plane online, and the experience can become unusable. I wrote about this last December after flying Delta to Las Vegas. The system repeatedly bogged down until nothing would load. I’d rather pay for internet that works than get free internet that doesn’t. Bandwidth has to be shared. Removing the price doesn’t create more capacity, but it gives a lot more people a reason to connect. A connection that works well with light use just isn’t the same thing – and Starlink’s low earth orbit satellites simply give the signal less distance to travel, delivering almost no latency. Bastian points to two new Viasat satellites. ViaSat-3 F3 entered service in August, and F2 entered service in September. But Delta’s own current wifi explanation acknowledges that performance varies with customer demand and satellite capacity, with less consistent service in high-demand or capacity-constrained areas. The airline knows this problem exists, which is why they’re touting Amazon’s service as a future improvement. United And Southwest Are Already Flying Starlink Bastian suggests most airlines promoting Starlink haven’t started yet. He doesn’t identify which airlines he’s counting. Here’s what the competitors actually say: United Airlines: More than half its daily flights already have Starlink. It expects nearly 64% by year-end and completion of installations by the end of 2027. Southwest Airlines: Its latest quarterly filing confirms equipped aircraft are already in service, with the full fleet expected to be finished in fall 2027. Last week it publicized gaming and livestreaming aboard a flight from Austin to San Diego. Alaska and Hawaiian: The group’s October 26 installation update shows all 93 Embraer 175s, Hawaiian’s 18 Airbus A321neos and 24 Airbus A330s equipped, along with 16 Boeing 737 MAX aircraft. Even Southwest expects to have Starlink throughout its fleet before Delta starts putting Amazon on its first 500 aircraft. That’s an awkward comparison for the airline charging a premium when it’ll be universal on the only U.S. airline without first class even. Wifi Doesn’t Have To Decide Every Ticket To Cost Delta Money I explained last month that I’ve avoided United and Southwest when I couldn’t count on functional internet. Starlink changes that calculation. I’ll pay more to work onboard because losing several productive hours costs more than the airfare savings. Recon Analytics finds wifi ranks among the top five business-trip airline selection factors for 32.6% of flyers, and first for 6.5%. Even among leisure travelers, 3.8% rank it first. Delta doesn’t need to lose everyone. It can lose a few expensive trips from customers who fly often, buy premium seats and carry airline credit cards. That’s precisely the business it wants. United is already using wifi to recruit those customers. It says its wifi-focused status match campaign produced a tenfold increase in daily applications. Amazon Still Has To Deliver. Bastian says that when Delta gets Amazon Leo, “we’ll be at least as good as Starlink if not better.” He hasn’t demonstrated that. Amazon needs enough satellites in the right orbits, working aircraft equipment, certification, and an airline installation program. It then has to deliver consistently with actual passengers using it. Delta’s own materials make the 2028 start subject to technical, certification and deployment milestones. And 2028 is the start of installations on an initial 500 aircraft. As I covered yesterday, Sunday’s failed Vulcan launch lost 40 Amazon satellites. We don’t yet know whether that pushes back Delta’s rollout. But the risk extends beyond replacing those satellites: Amazon contracted for 38 Vulcan missions to launch more than 1,500 of them. Amazon’s prelaunch photo shows the satellites stacked for that mission. Bastian’s account of testing Starlink is consistent with reporting from 2022. Delta had an early look at the product. It chose different commercial terms. I’ve covered the dispute over Delta’s branded portal. And last month Bastian said the branding disagreement out loud: “(Elon) thought it should be called Starlink on the planes. I said ‘No, it’s gotta be Delta.’” Amazon could offer a broader deal involving cloud computing and entertainment. Delta also gets to keep directing passengers through its own platform, where it promotes partners and sells them things. But a cheaper contract has to save enough to cover the business lost while passengers wait. If someone moves expensive flights to United, earns status there and starts spending on a United credit card, Delta may have to buy that loyalty back long after Amazon finally arrives. Last week it publicized gaming and livestreaming aboard a flight from Austin to San Diego. Alaska and Hawaiian: The group’s October 26 installation update shows all 93 Embraer 175s, Hawaiian’s 18 Airbus A321neos and 24 Airbus A330s equipped, along with 16 Boeing 737 MAX aircraft. Even Southwest expects to have Starlink throughout its fleet before Delta starts putting Amazon on its first 500 aircraft. That’s an awkward comparison for the airline charging a premium when it’ll be universal on the only U.S. airline without first class even. Wifi Doesn’t Have To Decide Every Ticket To Cost Delta Money I explained last month that I’ve avoided United and Southwest when I couldn’t count on functional internet. Starlink changes that calculation. I’ll pay more to work onboard because losing several productive hours costs more than the airfare savings. Recon Analytics finds wifi ranks among the top five business-trip airline selection factors for 32.6% of flyers, and first for 6.5%. Even among leisure travelers, 3.8% rank it first. Delta doesn’t need to lose everyone. It can lose a few expensive trips from customers who fly often, buy premium seats and carry airline credit cards. That’s precisely the business it wants. United is already using wifi to recruit those customers. It says its wifi-focused status match campaign produced a tenfold increase in daily applications. Amazon Still Has To Deliver. Bastian says that when Delta gets Amazon Leo, “we’ll be at least as good as Starlink if not better.” He hasn’t demonstrated that. Amazon needs enough satellites in the right orbits, working aircraft equipment, certification, and an airline installation program. It then has to deliver consistently with actual passengers using it. Delta’s own materials make the 2028 start subject to technical, certification and deployment milestones. And 2028 is the start of installations on an initial 500 aircraft. As I covered yesterday, Sunday’s failed Vulcan launch lost 40 Amazon satellites. We don’t yet know whether that pushes back Delta’s rollout. But the risk extends beyond replacing those satellites: Amazon contracted for 38 Vulcan missions to launch more than 1,500 of them. Amazon’s prelaunch photo shows the satellites stacked for that mission. Bastian’s account of testing Starlink is consistent with reporting from 2022. Delta had an early look at the product. It chose different commercial terms. I’ve covered the dispute over Delta’s branded portal. And last month Bastian said the branding disagreement out loud: “(Elon) thought it should be called Starlink on the planes. I said ‘No, it’s gotta be Delta.’” Amazon could offer a broader deal involving cloud computing and entertainment. Delta also gets to keep directing passengers through its own platform, where it promotes partners and sells them things. But a cheaper contract has to save enough to cover the business lost while passengers wait. If someone moves expensive flights to United, earns status there and starts spending on a United credit card, Delta may have to buy that loyalty back long after Amazon finally arrives. What customers consider to be “premium” is an ever changing thing. What exactly is so premium about Delta as compared to others? On time performance? It’s surely not the food. FAs are as much of a mixed bag as at UA/AA.

Even if DL wifi is usable, it’s certainly not thought of as premium. Starlink is simply excellent and is thought of as premium. Therefore, it would make sense for a brand that wants to be associated with the word premium to actually associate themselves with a brand that stands for premium and excellence.

The “it can’t also say Starlink” argument is absurd bunk. Maybe @TD will try to argue again that it doesn’t even say Airbus or Boeing on DL’s website (spoiler alert, it does).

The fact that DL did not choose Starlink is completely indefensible. Full stop. We know this to be the case because (other than B6, which barely counts) literally every other major airline in the world has signed on with Starlink. I think it’s around 50 of them at this point?

So DL is going to be an outlier… why? Because it’s CEO didn’t like having to bend the knee to Elon Musk? I mean, sure, personally, that’s a hard ask. But as a business matter? Not a close call.

So DL’s plan is to wait a few more years for Amazon to come online? Amazon may be many things, but it is not thought of as premium. It’s utilitarian. So even once that happens, they will have associated themselves with a non-premium brand. Why?

If DL wants folks to think of them as utilitarian, and wants to switch places with AA, that’s up to them I guess. But one would think the folks at Amex would be ringing alarm bells over this, and that someone at Amex is making some well placed phone calls to try and stop this madness.

Now, @TD will tell us that there’s no data anyone can point to, blah blah blah. What that has to do with brand perception is beyond me. And brand perception that translates into credit card spend is literally the entire ballgame!

@TD will also say that DL has more wifi throughout its fleet today or whatever and UA still doesn’t have Starlink on the widebodies, blah blah blah. How you can criticize a company for rapidly installing an excellent service throughout its fleet is beyond me. UA will be done installing Starlink in 2027, well before DL installs anything relating to Amazon – and does anyone seriously believe 2028 is achievable for more than a handful of installations just to say that they install something in 2028?

@Gary is 100% correct that Starlink will absolutely drive some consumer behavior here. And corporate behavior – shockingly corporations want their employees to have access at all times to internet that is high speed and works! DL’s actions here are borderline insane.

Is DL suddenly going to be unprofitable because of this? Of course not. Inertia is a powerful thing. But why DL would surrender an inch of premium association is beyond me. And that ultimately may have an impact on the bottom line – maybe not tomorrow, but in the weeks, months and years to come.

Finally, spare me the morality play. Competition is a good thing of course, and it’s good that Amazon is trying to be a viable competitor. But corporations have a responsibility to make sensible business decisions that enhance their profits, not to ensure competition. Amazon is simply not a competitor today. The airlines do everything possible to reduce competition at their hubs, they know the playbooks well. DL gets exactly zero moral brownie points for going with Amazon.

(Above is mostly copied from my comment this am at LALF.)

It’s not as though Delta’s wifi is going to be bad, it just won’t be anywhere near as good as its competitors and that’s where the VERY artificial delta premium brand starts to fall apart as customers start realizing how much is normal or worse at Delta vs competitors.

Delta still needs to work on replacing Gogo before they can even think about how great their ViaSat is. They’re way behind the industry in still even offering Gogo as a wifi product.

But trying to make the claim that ViaSat is as good as Starlink is just idiotic and even Delta knows that or they wouldn’t be upgrading already. ViaSat was much better than United’ satellite Panasonic when it rolled out and now Starlink is much better than Viasat. This isn’t that tough but a certain someone will probably lose his mind over this.

I’m aboard a Virgin transatlantic flight this moment using Starlink. Delta owns 49 % of Virgin and has no problem with it.

I have taken eight Delta flights in the last six weeks or so and every single one of them had a sizable amount of flight time where the WiFi was either unusably slow or downright nonfunctional (as in, lights off, no connection, nothing). A transcontinental from SFO to ATL during the morning/early afternoon — critical hours — saw the middle two hours of the flight with absolutely no connection. It’s in no way shape or form “fine” and it’s causing me to book away.

Hello from UA Starlink! The downside is I don’t have an excuse to be unproductive while working remote on a Tuesday, heh.

Perhaps this will be a moot debate in a few years and we can all enjoy free high speed WiFi on every flight but curious to see how this all plays out until then.
